blocks.text: Every monster in Unwritten is a **blank page** — one of the pages that should have carried the rest of the world's record and never did, given hostile form. That's why they appear **flat and papery**: their two-dimensional look isn't a style choice — it's what they *are*. To defeat one is to **fill it in**: one more line of the record that now exists because you wrote it.

items: **By biome** — each biome (Grassland, Snow, Desert, Volcanic, Corrupted) has its own family of monsters. See *World & Maps*.

**By level** — every monster has a level, exactly like you do. That single number is what makes it dangerous; there is no separate difficulty rating. Ordinary monsters and elites run from level 1 to 99, and the shadows from 105 to 160. A zone draws from a range of levels, so where a place sits in the world tells you what it will throw at you.

**By kind** — most monsters are ordinary. A few in each area are **elites**: stronger, and they keep calling ordinary monsters to their side. Stronger still are the twelve **shadows**, one for each weapon, each with a name of its own and gear at the highest grade — they call elites, and they are meant to take a whole guild to bring down. Anything a summoner calls gives nothing when it dies, and vanishes when its summoner does.

**By element** — a monster's element grows stronger with its kind: ordinary monsters are **level 1**, elites **level 2**, shadows **level 3**. Each shadow is Water, Earth, Fire or Wind, so the right converter answers every one of them (see *Combat Mechanics*).
**By size** — monsters are **Small, Medium, or Large**, which is meant to interact with your weapon type (see *Combat Mechanics*).

blocks.text: A monster is not built from a different set of numbers than you are. It has the **same six stats**, grown by the **same formulas**, and — this is the part that matters — it gets the **same number of stat points its level allows**. A level 20 monster is carrying exactly what a level 20 player could have bought. Nothing is inflated behind the scenes and nothing is quietly weakened.

items: **It wears real equipment** — the same gear you can wear, in the same slots. A monster's strength is its level, its stats, and its kit.
**It can carry Ring investment** — scaling it on the same soft-cap curve yours uses. A monster with a Ring behind it is a genuinely different fight.
**Its stats are visible in its numbers** — a monster that hits hard has the attack to prove it. There is no hidden multiplier making things tougher.

blocks.text: Because a monster is built like a character, anything a skill can do to you it can do to a monster — and the reverse. A monster can be slowed, shielded, guarded, drained, or pulled off its feet just as you can.

A monster **keeps what it wears** — its gear dies with it, because gear is made, not taken off a corpse. What it gives up is **materials**, **consumables** and **coin**. What falls lands on the ground where it died: for 10 seconds only the player who earned the kill can pick it up, then anyone can, and it vanishes after a minute if nobody does. Coin goes straight into your purse.

items: **Materials** — the metal, cloth and leather of the monster's own grade, which rises with its level, and now and then an **Ink** or a **Salt**. Elites drop far more, and rarer Inks and Salts; shadows more again. No stats of their own; they feed **Crafting & Recycling**.
**Consumables** — potions and food, now and then; a monster with an element also drops the **converters** of its own element.
**Bosses** are larger, self-assembled masses of blank page — absence gathered into something powerful and deliberate.
**The silencer** is the thing that stopped the scribe mid-sentence — the reason any page was left blank, and the deepest blankness in the world.
